# kiss-ssg

> A small, dependency-driven static site generator for Node. MVC-style: Handlebars views, JSON/HTTP/function models, JS controllers. ESM package (Node ≥22.12); engine in `lib/`, entry `lib/kiss.js`. No build step, no bundler.

Install: `npm install kiss-ssg --save-dev`. `import Kiss from 'kiss-ssg'` (CJS `require('kiss-ssg')` also works on Node ≥22.12). Everything is driven by a `Kiss` instance built with `new Kiss(config)` and used via a chainable API. Pages are queued (not rendered) by `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.scan()`; `.generate()` renders and writes them; `.sitemap()`/`.watch()` are opt-in extras. `config` and its resolved values are available in every view as `this.config`.

## The build script

Name it `router.js`, at the project root, and point `package.json`'s `main` and its `build`/`dev` scripts at it — and add `check` and `aikb` scripts beside them (`"check": "kiss-ssg check router.js"`, `"aikb": "kiss-ssg aikb router.js"`), so both are reachable as `npm run check` / `npm run aikb` rather than an `npx` form somebody has to remember. It is a router: `new Kiss(config)`, the `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.scan()` table, the terminal `.generate()`/`.sitemap()`/`.llms()`/`.feed()` chain, and the `complete()`/`catch()` pair. Custom helpers need no line here at all — kiss loads `config.folders.helpers` itself (tier 1 below). Everything else — helper bodies, the business's own facts, the completion callbacks once they outgrow a few lines — goes in a module beside it, so that reading the file answers "what pages does this site have, and where does each one's data come from" and nothing else. Name it that from the first commit even while it is one file: renaming it later is the change described under "three things that bite" below.

Each seam has **one trigger, and they are independent** — a site can reach tier 2 while its helpers are still at tier 0, and the tiers are not stages to pass through in order. Each trigger is a yes/no question with no judgement in it, deliberately: a threshold you have to adjudicate is one two readers will answer differently.

- **Tier 0 — one file.** Config, routes, the terminal chain. No custom helpers and no fact stated twice: nothing has been earned, so nothing is extracted. Most sites are born here and plenty stay. File length on its own never moves a site off tier 0 — a long router is a symptom to look at, not a trigger to act on.
- **Tier 1 — extract `helpers/`.** The moment the site has its **first** custom helper. Not three, not a proportion of the file: one. A helper that lives inside `router.js` cannot be imported, so it cannot be unit-tested, and that is true of the first one exactly as much as the fourth — testability is not a size question. The folder costs one file and one import; the migration you avoid by starting there is the expensive part. One module per _kind_ of thing (pure transformations, JSON-LD builders, anything derived from the page being rendered), each exporting a `register*Helpers(kiss)`, composed by an `index.js` that exports a single `registerHelpers(kiss)`. **You do not call it: kiss does.** `config.folders.helpers` defaults to `./helpers` beside the build script, and kiss imports that folder's `index.js` (or `.mjs`/`.cjs`) and calls its `registerHelpers` export — or its default export — itself. A site with no such folder is the ordinary case and says nothing. A folder that **breaks** — an entry that throws on import, or a registrar that throws — is a build failure named `<site helpers>`, because the alternative is every `{{helper}}` rendering as nothing on a green build. A folder whose entry exports no registrar **at all** depends on who chose the folder: if you set `folders.helpers`, that is a build failure too; if kiss defaulted to `./helpers`, it is a warning and the build continues, so a project that already had a root `helpers/` of unrelated utilities is not broken by the upgrade. Set `folders.helpers` to put it elsewhere, or to `null` if this site has none.

**It is watched in dev**, and an edit to that entry re-imports it on a cache-busted URL, re-registers, and re-renders every page — so a helper edit takes effect without a restart, the way an edited controller does; a helper the edited entry no longer registers is unregistered, and deleting the entry unregisters them all. A module the entry *imports* is the exception: ESM has no cache-invalidation API, so busting the entry's URL does not reach `./format.js`, and kiss prints the restart notice and does **not** rebuild rather than re-rendering against the cached copy and calling it done. Keeping it out of `src` is still the better shape for everything else the build script imports (the tier 2 `config/` below included): `src` is what `.watch()` watches for content and `folders` derives exactly six folders from it (`pages`, `assets`, `layouts`, `partials`, `models`, `controllers`), so a module in any *other* folder under `src` is none of those and every save triggers a whole-site replay that cannot pick the edit up — the module is already in the ESM cache and a replay never re-runs the build script. kiss prints a notice naming the restart rather than letting the rebuild imply it worked. Two exceptions, both because they have watchers of their own: `folders.assets` is re-copied, and `folders.helpers` is re-imported — so a helpers folder pointed inside `src` still works and is not nagged about.
- **Tier 2 — extract `config/` and the build report.** The moment one fact appears both in the markup a visitor reads and in the JSON-LD or feed metadata a machine reads (a phone number, a postal address, the social URLs), it belongs in a module the router spreads into `new Kiss()` as an arbitrary config key — which puts it on both sides at once, `{{config.business.telephone}}` in a template and `kiss.config.business` in a helper. When the `complete()`/`catch()` callbacks outgrow a few lines, they go to their own module too; a callback passed to `complete()` is invoked with `callback.call(this)`, so it must stay a `function` rather than an arrow if it reads `this.config` or `this.report()`.

Three things that bite:

- **Renaming an existing build script to `router.js` breaks references nothing will report.** A CSS toolchain's source globs, `package.json`'s `main` and scripts, a CI or host build command, and any `npx kiss-ssg check <script>` invocation all name the old file, and none of them fails loudly when it stops matching — a Tailwind `@source` that matches nothing is scanned in silence and its classes simply stop compiling. Rename, then grep the whole repo for the old name before building.
- **Export the pure function; register a thin adapter over it.** Moving a helper into `helpers/` buys nothing if its body still lives entirely inside the `register*Helpers(kiss)` closure — it is no more importable there than it was in the router. Export `buildBreadcrumb(pageURL, model, linkTo)` and let the registered helper be the three lines that unpack `options.data.root` and call it.
- **Helpers are registered once per process, so anything they read at registration time is frozen for the whole dev session.** A watch rebuild — including the one an edit to `router.js` itself triggers — replays the recorded `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.scan()` registrations on the same `Kiss` instance; it never re-imports the build script. A helper that reads a models folder with `fs.readdirSync` as it registers will still be serving that first reading after you have edited those models, and editing a helper module has no effect at all until you restart. Read the data inside the helper, at render time, and memoise it there if the cost matters.

## Building a site well

Five habits that separate a site that builds from a site that keeps working. They are short because
each one is checkable, and all five came from watching an agent convert a real site unaided.

- **Never hand-write an internal URL.** `{{link "about"}}` for a page, `{{asset "css/site.css"}}` for a
  file. Both fail the build when they are wrong, which is the entire reason to use them — a path you
  typed is a path nothing will ever check, and it breaks silently the first time a slug changes.
- **Content that repeats is data, not markup.** The same block appearing N times with different words
  is a JSON model and one partial, not N copies. Do it while you are writing it; the second copy is
  where drift starts, and later never comes.
- **`npx kiss-ssg check <script> --summary` is the bar, and the bar is zero broken links.** "It
  renders" is not a verdict. The check publishes nothing, so there is no reason not to run it.
- **Record the knowledge base when the work closes** (`npx kiss-ssg aikb <script>`) and commit it —
  and write the *retired-feedback* entries in `AIKB/site.md` while you still remember which decisions
  were contested and why. Nothing prompts you to do that, and it is the only thing that stops the next
  agent re-proposing what you just rejected. You will not remember tomorrow.
- **Read one example's page and its layout together**, not separately. `examples/4-layouts-and-partials/src/`
  is the smallest pair. The layout/page relationship is the one thing you cannot guess from a page
  alone, and reading them apart is how an hour disappears.

## API

- `.page(options)` — register one page. `options.view` (required): a `.hbs` filename relative to `config.folders.pages`, or a template string. `options.model`: a `.json` filename (relative to `config.folders.models`), an `http(s)://` URL (headers, timeout, retries and an on-disk cache come from `config.fetch`, below; a response with a non-2xx status fails that page — an error body is never used as the model, nor cached), a plain object, or a folder name (loads every `*.json` in it as an array). `options.controller`: a function `({model}) => optionsPatch`, or a `.js` filename relative to `config.folders.controllers`, run after the model resolves — commonly used to reshape/sort the model or derive `slug`. Controllers should stay pure: return new values rather than mutating `options.model` (or a nested object such as `options.config.folders`) in place. How much an in-place mutation costs you depends on the model kind — a `.json` file, a models folder, or an `http(s)://` URL model is re-resolved on every build and on every `.watch()` whole-site rebuild, so an in-place mutation of one of those is contained to that single build. A **plain object** model is different: it is replayed from a shallow snapshot of the original `.page()` call, so an object model (or a closed-over value) a controller mutated in place is still mutated on the next rebuild — an in-place `push`/assignment accumulates one more change per save, and the dev server drifts further from what a fresh build would produce with every edit. Returning new values sidesteps the distinction entirely. A controller that throws, a filename that does not exist, or a file that does not export a function fails that page and makes `complete()` reject. `options.title`, `options.description`, `options.path`, `options.slug`, `options.ext` (default `html`; a leading `.` is stripped and the rest slugified, so an `ext` derived from model data cannot steer the output path — `'.xml'` → `xml`, `'../x'` → `x`). `options.generate` (default `true`): set `false` to skip building this one page entirely — nothing is written, and it claims no output path, so it cannot collide with a page that is. `.generate()`/`.complete()` still resolve normally — the way to conditionally drop a page, e.g. a `.pages()` fan-out item that fails a check in its controller. `options.id`: this page's identity — what `{{link "<id>"}}` resolves (see `## Helpers`). It defaults to the view's route without its extension (`blog/listing.hbs` → `blog/listing`), so most pages need nothing; set it when you want a stable name (`id: 'blog'`) or when two `.page()` calls render one view (pagination), where **neither** gets the default id and a `notice` says so. On a `.pages()` fan-out an item's default id is the registration's route — or the registration's own `id`, used as a **prefix** — plus the item's slug (`blog/post/the-cascara-experiment`), and a *record* may carry its own `id`, which wins outright; the registration's `id` is never broadcast to the items, the same rule `aliases` follows. A controller may return one. Two pages claiming one explicit id fail the build (`Page id already claimed: <id>`), an explicit id beats a colliding default one, and a `generate: false` page claims no id at all. ``options.aliases`: old URL paths this page now answers (`aliases: ['/old-slug', '/news/2024/thing.html']`), each emitted as a `301` in the encoding `config.redirects.format` names — `<build>/_redirects` by default, plus the host-neutral `<build>/redirects.json` on every build that has one — see `## Checking a build`; on a `.pages()` fan-out the aliases belong to each **record**, never to the registration, so one item's `aliases` cannot be broadcast over the whole fan-out. `options.config`: per-page config overrides, merged over the global `config` for that page only — including `extensionLess`, which decides that page's output path, so one page on an `extensionLess` site can be written as a literal file (`config: { extensionLess: false }` with `slug: '404'` gives `404.html` rather than `404/index.html`, which is the filename Netlify and Cloudflare Pages look for and will not fall back from). Every page renders with its own shallow copy of the resolved config, so a controller mutating `options.config` changes that page alone — not the other pages, the instance's `config`, or the sitemap (nested objects such as `folders` are shared, and the engine never mutates them). `slug`/`path` are inferred from `view`'s file path if omitted — but only when `view` is a `.hbs` filename; a template string gets a random `snippet-N` slug and no path, since its own markup is not a file path. Slugs (and each `path` segment) are normalised by `utils.toSlug`: accented Latin is transliterated (`'Über uns'` → `uber-uns`), everything else outside `a-z0-9` becomes `-`, leading/trailing dashes are trimmed, and a title in a script with no Latin mapping (CJK, Hangul, Cyrillic) falls back to a short stable hash (`p-9736ca69`) so such pages stay distinct instead of all claiming one file. Two pages that resolve to the same output path **fail the build** (`complete()` rejects, naming the path) — only one of them would ever exist on disk.
- `.pages(options)` — same as `.page()`, but `options.model` must resolve to an array (or a models folder), and it fans out one page per item, appending `-N` to the slug per item unless the controller sets an explicit `slug`. A bad item fails only its own page: if the controller throws for one item the rest of the fan-out is still registered and built, and every bad item is reported separately by `complete()` as `<view> [item N: <slug>]` (no output path exists to name it by).
- `.scan()` — auto-discovers every `.hbs` under `config.folders.pages` you have not already registered (by `view`, so a `.page()` earlier in the same chain wins and the view is not built twice), and calls `.page()` on each with default options. The simplest way to build a whole site: `kiss.scan().generate()`. Under `.watch()` the scan is repeated on every whole-site rebuild, so page files you add or delete while the dev server runs are picked up.
- `.generate(callback)` — waits for every queued page's model to resolve, then renders and writes each page exactly once (in a normal build HTML is minified via `html-minifier-terser`, comments included; under `dev: true` minification is skipped altogether, so dev output keeps its comments and whitespace and a dev build never loads the minifier — **so a kiss build will never diff clean against output from a generator that does not minify**: migrating a site onto kiss, normalise both sides (drop comments, collapse inter-tag whitespace) before comparing, or every page reads as dozens of changed lines that are all `style="margin-top: 25px;"` becoming `style="margin-top:25px"`). `callback(data)` fires after every page has been attempted — including any that failed to render or write; page failures don't surface here, they surface via `complete()`. `data` is `[{ id, data }]`, one entry per queued promise **in registration order** — the automatic construction-time asset copy is queued first, so `data[0]` is that copy's result (`{ id, data: 'Copied assets: …' }`), not your first page. Use `getModelByID(id, data)` (below) rather than indexing by position. An error thrown by the callback itself (or a rejection from a promise it returns) is a build failure of its own, recorded as `<generate callback>` and reported by `complete()`. Chainable — returns the `Kiss` instance. To await the whole build use `await kiss.complete()`.
- `.complete(callback)` — resolves after every queued page and any `sitemap()` call has finished writing; resolves with the same `data` array `generate` receives. "Every queued page" includes pages queued from a `generate` callback, whether the callback queues them synchronously or after an `await` (the promise an `async` callback returns is part of what `complete()` waits for), and it includes any page queued after the last `generate()` call: `complete()` renders whatever no `generate()` pass reached, so a page whose model resolved late — or one a callback's `scan()` discovered — is never silently dropped from a build that reports success. It renders nothing if you never called `generate()` at all. Work a _synchronous_ callback defers to a later tick (a `setTimeout`-ed `.page()`) is still outside the build — queue pages synchronously, or from an `async` callback. Rejects with an `AggregateError` — `err.failures` = `[{ view, buildTo, error }]`, message `"N page(s) failed to build: <buildTo paths>"` (build paths, not views, since `.pages()` fan-out gives failed entries the same view; entries with no output path, such as a failing controller or callback, are named by `view` instead) — if any page failed to render or write, any controller failed, or a `generate`/`sitemap` callback threw; other pages still build, and the `generate` callback still fires. In `dev: true` a dev server that cannot bind `config.port` is a build failure too, reported as `<dev server>`; a redirects file that cannot be written is one as well, reported as `<redirects>` (a custom `redirects.format` writer that throws counts) (a site published without its redirects is a site whose old URLs 404), where a sitemap, `llms.txt` or feed write failure is only logged. It rejects **once per build**: a second `complete()` in the same build resolves instead of rejecting again, so the pattern of calling `complete()` from inside a `generate` callback cannot leave a second, unhandled rejection behind. A failed build never runs `complete()`'s own callback. A model failure is not a build failure: it is logged and skipped, and shows up in the resolved data as `{ id, data: null, error }`. A `.hbs` view whose file cannot be read (missing or misspelled) **is** a build failure: that page fails and `complete()` rejects, rather than the filename being written into the output.
- `.robots(options, callback)` — writes `robots.txt` to `config.folders.build`. Same lifecycle as `.sitemap()`, `.llms()` and `.feed()`: chainable, callable before or after `.generate()` and in any order relative to `.sitemap()`, waiting on the same internal queue, re-run by every whole-site `watch` rebuild. **The `Sitemap:` line is the point** — it is built by the same `toAbsoluteUrl` join as every `<loc>`, so the URL a crawler is pointed at is character-for-character the one `.sitemap()` wrote, and it follows `links.trailingSlash` with it. It is emitted **only when this build actually calls `.sitemap()`**, because advertising a sitemap that does not exist is a fetch error in every crawler that reads the line. Called with no options at all it writes one `User-agent: *` / `Allow: /` block plus that line, which is the file most sites hand-write minus the part they forget. `options.agents` is one block per crawler (`[{ userAgent, allow, disallow, crawlDelay }]`, where `allow`/`disallow` are a path or an array of them); `options.userAgent`/`allow`/`disallow` are the shorthand for a single block; `options.sitemap` is `true` (default), `false`, or a URL/path (or array) to advertise instead of this build's own; `options.overwrite` (default `true`) behaves exactly as the sitemap's, so `false` leaves a `robots.txt` you keep in `src/assets/` alone. A path containing whitespace is dropped rather than written, because one directive is one line. A write failure is logged and skipped, never a build failure — this is discovery, like the sitemap, not the redirects case. `report().robots` is `{ file, agents, disallowAll, sitemaps }`, or `null` when the method was never called. **`disallow: '/'` removes the site from search**: it logs a `notice` on every build that emits it and sets `disallowAll`, so a staging crawl policy reaching production is visible in a `kiss-ssg check` diff. It is never inferred — `ignoreSitemap` deliberately does **not** imply a `Disallow`, because blocking a crawler stops it seeing a `noindex` and can leave the URL indexed with no snippet. `callback(text)` receives the rendered file.

- `.report()` — the last settled build as data, or `null` before the first `.complete()` has settled (a watch rebuild replaces it with its own). `{ ok, mode, buildDir, duration, pages, failures, assets, sitemap, pipeline, llms, aikb, links, redirects, feed, robots }`: `ok` is "nothing failed"; `mode` is `'build'`, or `'check'` when the build was staged and thrown away (see `## Checking a build`); `buildDir` is the folder you asked for, never the staging sibling a `'atomic'` build writes to; `duration` is ms from `new Kiss()`; `pages` is `{ view, buildTo, ok, hash, id }` per queued page, in registration order (an inline template's `view` is elided to its first line; `hash` is the sha1 of the bytes that page wrote, or `null` when it wrote none — a page that failed, or one with `generate: false`; `id` is the page's identity, what `{{link}}` resolves, and is `null` for an inline template, a `generate: false` page and a default id two pages arrived at); `failures` is `{ view, buildTo, message }` — the same list `err.failures` carries, with the `Error` reduced to its message so the whole thing survives `JSON.stringify`; `assets` is `{ source, target }` per emitted file (the path a template asks for, and the file that is actually there under `config.assets`); `sitemap` is the `sitemap.xml` this build wrote, or `null`; `pipeline` is `{ name, ok, duration }` per `config.assets.pipeline` step, in order, and `[]` when there are none; `llms` is the `llms.txt` this build wrote, or `null`; `aikb` is `null` unless the site has a knowledge base to report on (`config.folders.aikb` set, and a record already made — see `## Checking a build`), and otherwise `{ folder, written, notes: { missing, dead, stale, dangling }, subjects }` — where that knowledge base lives, whether this build wrote it (`true` only for a passing `npx kiss-ssg aikb` run; every ordinary build reports `false`), the four note findings (paths, except `dangling`'s `<note path>: <token>`), and `{ kind, id, note, hash }` per subject of *this* build, which is where the hash to stamp a note with comes from before a record has been made. The same object is on the rejection as `err.report`, so a failed build is readable as data without catching and re-deriving anything. `links`, `redirects` and `feed` are **new in this version**, appended in that order after `aikb`, and each is `null` until the build in question did that piece of work — which is not the same as "it did it and found nothing". `links` carries the broken-internal-link scan of this build's own output as `{ checked, broken: [{ page, href }] }` (`null` on a dev build, on a watch rebuild and under `config.links.check: false`); `redirects` carries what the build did about page `aliases` as `{ file, aliases, removed, collisions, moved, rules, json, format, files }` — the host file it wrote (`null` under `format: 'none'`), how many alias paths went into it, **`rules`, the resolved `[{ from, to }]` list** so a deploy script can write any host's format from `kiss.report()` without parsing anything, the `redirects.json` IR, the format that ran, every file written, the pages the last record had that this build no longer has and no alias covers, the aliases a live page already answers, and `{ id, from, to }` per page the record and this build share an `id` with whose path changed and whose old path no alias covers; `feed` is the feed file this build wrote, like `sitemap` and `llms`; `robots` is `{ file, agents, disallowAll, sitemaps }` from `.robots()`, or `null` when it was never called — an object rather than a path because `disallowAll` is a fact that removes the site from search and a path cannot say it. Every path in the three is named against the build folder you asked for, never the staging sibling. It is additive: `complete()` still resolves with the `data` array and still rejects with the `AggregateError`.
- `.sitemap(options, callback)` — writes `sitemap.xml` to `config.folders.build`, derived from every registered page. Requires `config.siteUrl` (logs an error and skips, does not throw, if unset). Can be called before or after `.generate()` — both just wait on the same internal promise queue. Per-page opt-out: `ignoreSitemap: true` in that page's `.page()`/`.pages()` options; a `generate: false` page is left out too. Per-page overrides: `sitemapPriority` (default `'1.00'`), `sitemapChangefreq` (omitted from the XML unless set), `sitemapLastmod` (default: one timestamp shared by all pages, captured when `.sitemap()` runs). **That default makes `sitemap.xml` the one artefact an otherwise byte-stable build changes on every run** — every page reads as "changed just now", which is no signal to a crawler and a standing diff for a site that commits its output. Set `sitemapLastmod` per page (from the source's own date, or a record's) to get a stamp that means something and a reproducible file. `options.overwrite` (default `true`) — set `false` to skip (re)writing if `sitemap.xml` already exists; only has an effect if `cleanBuild: false` too, since the default `cleanBuild: true` already empties the whole build dir — including any prior `sitemap.xml` — before `.sitemap()` ever runs.
- `.llms(options, callback)` — writes `llms.txt` to `config.folders.build`: the [llmstxt.org](https://llmstxt.org) index an answer engine reads first, derived from the same registry the sitemap is. Same lifecycle as `.sitemap()` — chainable, callable before or after `.generate()`, waiting on the same internal queue, and re-run by every whole-site `watch` rebuild. `options.title` (required) is the file's `# ` heading; `options.summary` (required) is the `> ` blockquote, and is either the text itself or a path (relative to `process.cwd()`) to a `.md`/`.txt` file holding it; `options.notes` (optional, same text-or-file rule) becomes a trailing `## Notes` section; `options.sections` maps a top-level path segment to a heading (`{ courses: 'Courses' }`, the key `root` naming the section that holds pages with no path, default `Pages`), and an unmapped segment is title-cased; `options.overwrite` (default `true`) behaves exactly as the sitemap's. A missing `config.siteUrl`, `title` or `summary` logs an error and skips the file — it never throws, and the callback does not fire. Pages are grouped by the first segment of their `path` (root pages first) and listed in registration order as `- [title](url): description`, with the description omitted when the page has none and the title falling back to the page's slug, title-cased. Each URL is the **same string** the page's own `{{canonical}}` and its `<loc>` in `sitemap.xml` are, built by the same code. Per-page: `ignoreLlms: true` keeps a page out; `ignoreSitemap: true` and `generate: false` keep it out automatically; `llmsSection: 'Name'` overrides the group it lands in. `callback(text)` receives the rendered file.
- `.feed(options, callback)` — writes an RSS 2.0 feed to `config.folders.build`: the third file derived from the same registry as `sitemap.xml` and `llms.txt`, so an item can never name a URL the site does not serve. Same lifecycle as `.sitemap()` and `.llms()` — chainable, callable before or after `.generate()`, waiting on the same internal queue, and re-run by every whole-site `watch` rebuild. `options.title` (required) is the channel's `<title>`; `options.description` is its `<description>`; `options.section` limits the feed to one top-level `path` segment (`{ section: 'blog' }` — omit it for every page); `options.limit` (default `20`) caps the items; `options.filename` (default `feed.xml`) names the file inside the build folder (a name that resolves outside it is refused); `options.dateField` (default `'date'`) names the field each item's date comes from; `options.overwrite` (default `true`) behaves exactly as the sitemap's. A missing `config.siteUrl` or `title` logs an error and skips the file — it never throws, and the callback does not fire. **One item per page that carries a date**, newest first (the URL breaks a tie), where the date is `options[dateField] ?? options.model[dateField]` — so a post can be dated in its `.page()`/`.pages()` options or in its model, and either way it is the same field. A `Date`, epoch milliseconds, or any string `new Date()` parses is accepted; a value that cannot be read logs one warning and the page is treated as undated. Pages with no date are simply left out, silently — most of a site is undated. Per-page: `ignoreFeed: true` keeps a page out; `ignoreSitemap: true` and `generate: false` keep it out automatically. Each `<link>`/`<guid>` is the **same string** as the page's own `{{canonical}}` and its `<loc>` in `sitemap.xml`; `<title>` and `<description>` are derived exactly as `llms.txt` derives them. `<lastBuildDate>` is the newest item's date rather than the wall clock, so two identical builds produce byte-identical files. `report().feed` names the file written (against the build folder you asked for, never a staging sibling), or `null`. `callback(text)` receives the rendered document.
- `.watch(options)` — starts a `chokidar` watcher on `config.folders.src` (only meaningful with `dev: true`, which also starts a livereload dev server on `config.port`, default `3001`, bound to `config.devHost`, with live reload on `config.livereloadPort`); rebuilds just the affected page(s), or the whole site if a changed file can't be matched to a queued page. Editing a partial or a layout re-registers the partials and re-renders **only the pages that rendered it** — learned at render time, so a partial chosen with `lookup`, reached through another partial, or used as a layout all count — without re-resolving any model (URL models included) or re-running any controller; a partial no page has rendered yet re-renders every page and logs a notice naming it. With `verbose: true` a dev build also writes `dependency-graph.json` (`{ partial: [built pages…] }`) beside `debug.json`, and each page's `.json` sibling lists the `partials` it used. Every other non-page change is a whole-site rebuild. A whole-site rebuild replays every `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.scan()` registration from scratch, so edited models and controllers take effect (controller files are reloaded from disk, ESM and CommonJS alike) — which means every URL model is fetched again on every rebuild unless you set `config.fetch.cache`; a single-page rebuild is a template re-render. A whole-site rebuild also deletes output files the previous build wrote that the new one no longer produces (a removed fan-out model, a changed slug, or a page `.scan()` had discovered whose `.hbs` file you deleted — a page you registered by name instead keeps failing the build until you remove the call) and re-runs `.sitemap()` if you ever called it. Creating a file under `src/` rebuilds the whole site too, so a partial or layout you add mid-session is registered and usable straight away (a file created empty is picked up once it has content — an event on an empty file is ignored, which is also what keeps a slow truncate-then-write save from rebuilding against a half-written file), and a new page `.hbs` is built as well if you used `.scan()` (a rebuild scans the pages folder again; on an explicitly registered site you still add the `.page()` call yourself). Deleting a partial or layout unregisters it, so any page still referencing it fails the rebuild with `The partial <name> could not be found` instead of quietly rendering the deleted content until you restart. `options.entry` (default `process.argv[1]`): the script whose change triggers a full rebuild. The browser is told to reload **once per rebuild, after every page has been written** (and once when the first build finishes), never once per file — so a reload can never land on a page the rebuild has not re-rendered yet. An edited stylesheet reloads that stylesheet alone, leaving the page's state alone.
- `.close()` — stops the file watcher and dev server (dev mode / after `.watch()`); returns a Promise that resolves once any in-flight rebuild has finished, so nothing is written after it.
- `.copyAssets(sourceDir, targetDir)` — compiles every `*.scss`/`*.sass` under `sourceDir` to a sibling `.css` and copies everything else straight through to `targetDir`. Runs automatically once at construction time for `config.folders.assets` → `config.folders.build`; callable again for extra asset directories. Calls run one after another in registration order, not concurrently. Every emitted file is recorded in the instance's asset manifest — that is what `{{asset}}` reads, and what `config.assets` renames (see `## Config`).
- `.registerPartials()` — re-registers every partial and layout from disk, unregistering any name whose file has since gone. **The registered extensions are exactly `.hbs`, `.html`, `.md` and `.txt` under `folders.partials`, and `.hbs` under `folders.layouts`** — a file with any other extension is not a partial, and `{{> "name"}}` for it fails the build with `The partial name could not be found`. **The extension says what happens to the file**: `.hbs` is a template, `.md` is Markdown rendered to HTML, `.html` is inserted as-is, and `.txt` is *text* — escaped exactly as `{{ }}` escapes a value and **not compiled**, so its markup is shown rather than rendered and `{{name}}` inside it is printed rather than interpolated. That is what makes a code sample work: `<pre>{{> "snippet"}}</pre>` with `snippet.txt` holding `<div class="card">{{title}}</div>` shows that line, tags, braces and all. The other three are compiled as Handlebars templates (`.md` after its Markdown is rendered), so `{{` in one of those **is** interpolated. Names are path-derived and extension-less, so `note.txt` and `note.hbs` would collide and the template wins. Returns the list of registered names. **Every entry of `kiss.handlebars.partials` is a function** — a compiled template that also records which page invoked it, which is what scopes a watch-mode partial edit to the pages that used it. `handlebars-layouts` recompiles a string layout on every page render and never caches it, so compiling at registration is also what stops a layout being recompiled once per page. Code of yours that renders an entry by name must accept a function, and must pass its own `options.data` through: `const p = kiss.handlebars.partials[name]; typeof p === 'function' ? p(ctx, { data: options.data }) : kiss.handlebars.compile(p)(ctx, { data: options.data })` (it was a string only until the partial's first render anyway). That data frame is how the page is recorded as using the partial: a bare `p(ctx)` renders correctly, but under `.watch()` that page is not re-rendered when the partial changes (unless no page recorded it at all, when every page is). Runs automatically at construction and on every watch rebuild — call it yourself to pick up partials added or removed at runtime outside `.watch()`. A `.md` or `.html` partial is a Handlebars template like any other: the built-in and registered helpers run inside it (`{{asset "js/site.js"}}` in a `.html` partial resolves), and its `.md` body is rendered to HTML first.
- `.viewStats()` — logs the queued-promise and prepared-page counts, and (with `verbose: true`) writes `debug.json` — one entry per page, `{ view, buildTo, runCount, options }` — into `config.folders.build`. Chainable; use it from a `generate` callback to see what a build actually produced.
- `.getModelByID(id, data)` — looks an entry up by `id` in the `[{ id, data }]` array `generate`/`complete` hand back, and returns its `.data` (or `{ error }` if there is no such id). The `id` is the model filename or URL you passed; object models get a hash instead. Use it to pull one page's resolved model out of the build data.
- `kiss.handlebars` — this instance's own Handlebars environment (`Handlebars.create()`, created per `Kiss`, so helpers and partials never leak between instances, and helpers registered on the global `handlebars` module are not seen); register custom helpers on it directly. Built-in helpers (`markdown`, `sass`, `offset`, `stringify`, `lookup`, `isActive`, `canonical`, `absUrl`, `asset`, `link`, `env`) are documented in `## Helpers` below. The block renders with the surrounding context **plus** the hash, the hash winning on a clash — so `{{#each nav}}{{#isActive ../page href=href}}{{label}}{{/isActive}}{{/each}}` sees the item's `label`, and `active`, `href`, `folderMatch` and `pageURL` are always the helper's own.
- `kiss.remarkable` — this instance's own Markdown renderer (used for `.md` partials and the `markdown` helper).
- `import { utils } from 'kiss-ssg'` — `toSlug`, `sanitizePath`, `toTitleCase`, `trimLines`, `trimPath`, `posixPath`, `globFiles(dir, pattern)`, `hashId`, `toURLKey`, `toAbsoluteUrl(siteUrl, path, { trailingSlash })`, `toCanonicalPath`, `servedPathFor(pageURL, { trailingSlash })`.
- `import { renderRedirects, renderRedirectsJson, renderFirebaseRedirects, renderVercelRedirects, renderHtaccessRedirects } from 'kiss-ssg'` — the redirect encoders, each `(rules) => string` over the same `[{ from, to }]` a custom `redirects.format` writer is handed. Exported so a writer can **compose** a shipped encoding (take Netlify's exact bytes, write them somewhere else, append a rule of your own) rather than reimplementing one kiss already has.

## Config

Passed to `new Kiss(config)`. Defaults:

```js
{
  dev: false,          // starts a livereload dev server + file watcher; skips minification
  verbose: false,
  cleanBuild: true,     // true | false | 'atomic' — see below; true empties config.folders.build in the constructor
  extensionLess: false, // true: non-index pages build to <path>/<slug>/index.html instead of <path>/<slug>.html
  siteUrl: undefined,   // required by .sitemap() and the canonical/absUrl helpers
  sass: { includePaths: [] },
  fetch: {              // policy for http(s) models (per instance, not per page)
    headers: {},        // sent with every URL-model request (auth, accept)
    timeout: 10000,     // ms; the request is aborted and the page fails
    retries: 0,         // extra attempts on a network error or a 5xx; a 4xx is never retried
    cache: false,       // or a directory: successful bodies are cached there, keyed by url + headers
  },
  assets: {             // policy for the files copyAssets emits; all off = today's build
    hash: false,        // true: every emitted .css/.js is renamed to carry a content hash
    version: null,      // a string: nothing is renamed, {{asset}} appends ?v=<string>
    pipeline: [],       // ordered { name?, run, watch?, cwd? } commands run before the asset copy
  },
  markdown: {           // Remarkable options for .md partials and the {{markdown}} helper
    html: true,         // render raw HTML in the source rather than escaping it
    xhtmlOut: true,     // close single tags XHTML-style (<br />)
    breaks: false,      // true: every newline inside a paragraph becomes a <br />
  },
  links: {              // the broken-internal-link scan, and what {{link}} emits
    check: true,        // false: skip the scan; the finding is advisory either way
    canonical: false,   // true: bare {{link}} emits /about, not /about.html
    trailingSlash: true,// false: a directory index is /courses, not /courses/ — host policy, see below
  },
  redirects: {          // how page aliases are emitted; redirects.json is always written
    format: null,       // no host file. 'netlify' | 'firebase' | 'vercel' | 'htaccess' | a writer fn,
                        // or an ARRAY of those: ['netlify','firebase'] emits both
  },
  port: 3001,           // dev server port
  livereloadPort: 35729, // live reload port; also the port injected into the dev-mode reload <script>
  devHost: '127.0.0.1',  // interface the dev + live reload servers bind to
  folders: {
    src: './src',
    pages: './src/pages',
    build: './public',
    assets: './src/assets',
    layouts: './src/layouts',
    partials: './src/partials',
    models: './src/models',
    controllers: './src/controllers',
    aikb: './AIKB',   // where `kiss-ssg aikb` records the site's knowledge base; source-side, committed, and not derived from src
    helpers: './helpers', // the site's own Handlebars helpers: kiss imports this folder's `index.js` and calls its `registerHelpers(kiss)` export, so the build script never registers them itself. Beside the build script, not derived from `src`, not created for you, and watched in dev so an edit re-imports and re-renders.
  },
}
```

`cleanBuild` decides what happens to `config.folders.build`. `true` (the default) empties it with `fs.emptyDirSync` **in the `Kiss` constructor** — before any model resolves and before any page renders — and nothing puts it back if the build then fails, so a failed re-run leaves the folder empty or half-built. `false` never cleans, and stale files from earlier builds stay. `'atomic'` builds into a staging sibling (`<build>.kiss-staging-<pid>-<random>`) and swaps the whole folder into place only when `complete()` resolves: until that moment the previous output is untouched, a build that fails (or that you never `complete()`) leaves it exactly as it was, and `close()` removes the staging folder. Pages, assets, `sitemap.xml` and `debug.json` all follow the staging folder, including a `.copyAssets()` you aimed explicitly at the build folder. The swap is two renames (the old folder is renamed aside, staging is renamed in, then the old one is deleted), so the previous output is never gone while a copy is in progress, and a build that is killed mid-flight leaves a `<build>.kiss-staging-…` / `.kiss-old-…` sibling that the next run removes with one notice. `'atomic'` is for one-shot builds: in `dev: true` it degrades to `true` (the dev server serves the build folder from the start) and logs one notice saying so. **The consequence, which is the part that bites: a dev run writes its output into `folders.build` like any other build, so if that folder is what you publish (GitHub Pages' `./docs`, a committed `public/`), one `npm run dev` leaves a dev build in the published folder** — carrying the injected livereload `<script>`, expanded rather than compressed CSS, no HTML minification, and the per-page `.json` siblings. Point dev at a different, git-ignored `build` folder (`build: dev ? './.kiss-dev' : './docs'`) rather than relying on remembering, and only `complete()` promotes — a chain that ends at `.generate()` never swaps anything in. Any other value throws. **If `config.folders.build` points at published output** — an archive of per-version builds, say — use `'atomic'`, and validate the folder name before you construct: an empty string interpolated into the path resolves to the parent folder, and `true` would empty the whole archive at construction. kiss refuses one shape of that at construction whatever `cleanBuild` says: a `build` folder that **is, or contains, the source folder** throws, since cleaning it would delete the site's own source. That is one rule, not two — `build: '.'` throws for the ordinary layout because `./src` is inside it, not because `'.'` is a filesystem root. A `build` that is a repository root with its `src` somewhere outside is permitted.

**Building more than one site from one source tree**: kiss has no "versions" concept — it is one `Kiss` instance per `folders.build`. An archive of per-version outputs (per-intake handbooks, a menu rebuilt each season) needs only: one `Kiss` per output with `folders.build` as the discriminator (`build: './menus/' + season`); an arbitrary config key carried into views as the per-build variable (`new Kiss({ season, ... })` read as `{{config.season}}`); `folders.assets: null` plus an explicit `copyAssets(src, buildDir)` when each output must own its assets rather than share a folder kiss keeps re-copying from; and `cleanBuild: 'atomic'` so a re-run fixing one output can never destroy or half-build another already published. Validate the value before it reaches `folders.build` — an empty or malformed one resolves against the parent of every output already there. See **Cleaning the build folder** above and `examples/7-versioned-outputs/router.js`.

`fetch` is the policy for `http(s)` models. `headers` goes out with every URL-model request — an `Authorization` header for an API that needs one, an `Accept` header for an API that offers several shapes. `timeout` (ms) aborts a request that never answers and fails that page rather than hanging the build; it is the one default with teeth, since before it existed a silent upstream stalled a build for ever. `retries` adds attempts after a network error or a 5xx, with a short linear backoff — a 4xx is never retried, because the server has already told you the request itself is wrong, and the rejection names how many attempts were made. `cache` is `false` or a directory path: a successful body is written there under a hash of the URL **and** the header set (a different token is a different entry), and every later resolution of that URL — later in this build, in the next `.watch()` rebuild, or in tomorrow's build in a new process — reads the file instead of fetching. A cached model is a build input, exactly like a `.json` file in `folders.models`: it makes `dev` mode and watch rebuilds stop paying a network round trip per remote model, and it lets an offline build work. There is no TTL — delete the directory (or one file in it) to refetch — and it is build output, so add it to `.gitignore`. An error response is never cached: the non-2xx guard stays authoritative over the cache. The block is merged one level deep, like `sass`, and applies per `Kiss` instance — there is no per-page override.

`assets` is the cache-busting policy for the files `.copyAssets()` emits, and it is read by the `{{asset}}` helper (below). With both keys at their defaults a build emits exactly the files and paths it always did. `hash: true` renames every emitted `.css` and `.js` to carry an 8-character hash of its **emitted** bytes (`css/site.css` → `css/site.a1b2c3d4.css`, and a `.scss` is hashed after sass compiled it), so a changed file is a new URL a cache has never seen and an unchanged one keeps its URL; the old file is deleted as the new one is written, so a watch-mode edit leaves one stylesheet in the build, not one per save. Nothing else is renamed — an image, a font or `robots.txt` is reached by URLs kiss does not rewrite (the ones inside a stylesheet, the ones a host asks for by a fixed name) — but every copied file is in the manifest, so `{{asset}}` resolves them all. `version: '1.4.5'` is the alternative: no file is renamed and `{{asset}}` appends `?v=1.4.5` instead, which suits a host that would rather not see new filenames. Setting both is a misconfiguration — the hashed filename wins and a warning says so. The block is merged one level deep, like `sass` and `fetch`, and applies per `Kiss` instance: the files are emitted once, so there is no per-page override.

`assets.pipeline` is how a site runs an external tool as part of the build — a CSS toolchain, an icon sprite, anything with a command line. Each step is `{ name?, run, watch?, cwd? }`. Every `run` is executed through a shell, in order, awaited, **before** the asset copy, so a tool that writes into the assets folder (`src/assets/css/site.css`) has its output copied into the build like any other asset — and again before the copy on every whole-site `watch` rebuild. A step that exits non-zero (or cannot be spawned) is a build failure like a failed page: `complete()` rejects, the failure is named `<pipeline: <name>>` in `err.failures`, and the pages and the asset copy still run so the whole build is still reported. `name` defaults to the first word of `run`; `cwd` defaults to `process.cwd()`; each command inherits `process.env` plus `KISS_BUILD`, `KISS_ASSETS` and `KISS_DEV` (`'1'`/`'0'`). `watch` is the dev-mode half: in `dev: true` only, it is started once after that step's `run` succeeded, kept for the session with its output going through the logger, and ended by `close()` — it is not started again by a rebuild, and a watch process that dies on its own is logged, not a build failure. Tailwind, end to end:

```js
assets: {
  pipeline: [
    {
      name: 'tailwind',
      run: 'npx @tailwindcss/cli -i src/styles/site.css -o src/assets/css/site.css --minify',
      watch: 'npx @tailwindcss/cli -i src/styles/site.css -o src/assets/css/site.css --minify --watch=always',
    },
  ],
}
```

**Two traps in that command, both silent, and an agent writing a Tailwind site should assume it will hit them.** They are why the `-i` is there and why the recipe above is not the whole story.

*Tailwind scans more than you think, and with `assets.hash` that moves every page's `<link>`.* Tailwind v4 walks the **whole project** for class-name candidates — everything not excluded by `.gitignore`, `node_modules`, a lockfile, a binary or a CSS file — and `@source` **adds** to that walk rather than replacing it. A site that writes an explicit `@source` list, reasonably reading it as *the* source list, is still scanning its own `.md`, `.txt` and JSON. Tailwind treats every file as plain text, so an ordinary English word is a candidate class: with `assets.hash: true` the stylesheet's content hash **is** its filename, so typing the word `invisible` into a tracked `README.md` compiles `.invisible{visibility:hidden}`, renames `css/site.<hash>.css`, and changes the `<link href>` on **every** page — `check` then reports the whole site as `~ N changed, = 0 unchanged` with nothing in the page sources to explain it. Measured on Tailwind 4.3.3: that one word took the stylesheet 4,381 → 4,410 bytes. What makes it cost days rather than minutes is that it is **intermittent** — a word only counts if it forms a clean candidate token, so `capitalize` in prose compiles while `capitalize.` and `capitalize,` (trailing punctuation) do not, and a word matching an already-compiled utility changes nothing. So the hash moves on some documentation edits and not others, with no visible pattern. Turn the walk off and list the real sources:

```css
@import 'tailwindcss' source(none);
@source '../views'; /* resolved against THIS stylesheet's folder, not the cwd */
@source '../partials';
```

A `@source` path that resolves to nothing is silent too: `source(none)` with `@source './index.html'` written in `src/styles/site.css` looks for `src/index.html`, matches nothing, and compiles an empty utility layer rather than erroring.

A guard is worth more than the doc here, because both failures are silent and both produce a plausible file. A few lines in the build — run as a `pipeline` step or in CI — that fail when `source(none)` is missing from the entry stylesheet, or when any `@source` path no longer resolves, catch the whole class: the accidental re-enabling of the walk, and the silently-empty `@source` above. It needs nothing built and is what caught this on a real site.

*Keep the `-i`.* `npx @tailwindcss/cli -o out.css` with no `-i` **exits 0**, prints a normal timing line and writes a plausible stylesheet — but it never reads your entry file. The CLI substitutes a default input of `@import 'tailwindcss'`, so the loss is not a few rules, it is **everything you authored**: every `@layer components` class, every `@theme` token, every `@font-face`, every plugin import and every `@source` line. Verified on 4.3.3 — an entry file declaring `.btn`, `.card`, `.callout` and a self-hosted `@font-face` compiled all of them with `-i` and **none** of them without. On a real 20-page site the output fell from 66,384 to 24,990 bytes; what survives is generic utilities. It is dangerous precisely because nothing fails, and a project whose dev command passes `-i` while its build command does not is correct on every developer's machine and wrong only on the deployed site — which is how it survives for months.

`kiss-ssg check` runs the pipeline exactly as a build does, so a check is not read-only over your working tree: it regenerates whatever the steps generate (their output is a source file, which is why there is nothing extra for the check to discard). Scoped re-renders — a page view, a partial or a layout edit under `watch` — deliberately do **not** re-run the steps; a tool that must see those edits is what `watch` is for. A watch command gets no stdin from kiss, so a tool that stops when stdin closes needs its keep-alive flag — Tailwind's is `--watch=always`; plain `--watch` exits at once and the log says `pipeline watch "tailwind" exited (code 0)`. `examples/10-asset-pipeline/router.js` is the runnable version of all of this.

`markdown` is the option set handed to this instance's Remarkable — the renderer behind both `.md` partials and the `{{markdown}}` helper — so the two can never disagree. The three keys above are the ones kiss has a default for, **not** the ones it accepts: the block is passed through as-is, so any other Remarkable option (`typographer: true`, `langPrefix`) reaches the renderer without kiss knowing the name. `breaks: false` is deliberate and matches published v1: with `breaks: true` a paragraph hard-wrapped in the source renders one `<br />` per source line, breaking prose mid-sentence at whatever column the author happened to wrap at — set it to `true` only if your `.md` sources treat a newline as a real line break. Merged one level deep, like `sass`, `fetch` and `assets`, so `markdown: { breaks: true }` keeps `html` and `xhtmlOut` at their defaults. It applies per `Kiss` instance and is read in the constructor, **before** partials are registered: `.md` partials are rendered to HTML at registration, so setting it in config is the only way to reach them — mutating `kiss.remarkable` afterwards would change the helper but silently miss every partial (a later `kiss.registerPartials()` is what that would need).

`livereloadPort` lets two sites run side by side: give the second one its own value, or its pages would poll the first site's live reload server. A clash on the live reload port is logged and live reload is switched off for that site — the dev server keeps serving. A clash on `port` is fatal instead: nothing can be served without the HTTP server, so the bind failure is reported exactly once (`Dev server could not bind 127.0.0.1:3001 (EADDRINUSE): the site is not being served`), the watcher and live reload are closed so the process can exit, and `complete()` rejects with a `<dev server>` failure. The `Serving …` line is printed only once the server is actually listening. Use `port` (with its own `livereloadPort`) to run a second site. `devHost` binds the dev and live reload servers to loopback only; set it to `'0.0.0.0'` to open the preview to other devices on your network — live reload follows the host the page was loaded from, so a preview opened on a phone reloads from the machine serving it.

A key you pass explicitly as `undefined` takes its default (`port: process.env.PORT` with `PORT` unset gives 3001); `null` is a real value — it switches a folder off.

Setting `folders.src` re-derives `pages`, `assets`, `layouts`, `partials`, `models` and `controllers` from it (`${src}/${key}`), unless a given key is also set explicitly in the same `folders` object — `build` is independent and always defaults to `./public` regardless of `src`. Folder strings are normalised on the way in — a trailing slash or a backslash separator is tolerated (`'./src/assets/'` and `'.\\src\\assets'` both resolve to `'./src/assets'`).

## Host URL policy

Two things kiss emits are decided by your host, not by the generator, and both are config keys whose defaults are what kiss has always done. A site author cannot discover either until the site is deployed and the redirect chain is live, which is why they are written down here.

**The trailing slash on a directory index** (`links.trailingSlash`, default `true`). Measured live on 2026-09-16:

| Host                                                         | `/courses/` (dir index) | `/about` (file page) |
| ------------------------------------------------------------ | ----------------------- | -------------------- |
| Netlify — verified on `www.a1k9training.co.uk`                 | 200; bare `/courses` 301s to it | 200; `/about/` 301s to it |
| Firebase Hosting, `cleanUrls: true` + `trailingSlash: false` — verified on `learna.ac.uk` | 301 to `/courses`; the **bare** form is 200 | 200; `/about/` 301s to it |
| Cloudflare Pages, GitHub Pages, nginx                          | **unverified** — has a trailing-slash mode; check your deployment rather than assuming | unverified |

The two verified hosts agree on file pages and contradict each other on directory indexes, so kiss cannot be right for both: `trailingSlash: true` (the default) matches Netlify, `false` matches that Firebase configuration. The setting moves **every** URL kiss derives for a page together — `{{canonical}}`, `{{link}}`'s href, `<loc>`, the `llms.txt` entry, the feed `<link>` and an alias's target — because a page advertised at two spellings ships a redirect on every internal click. It does **not** move `{{isActive}}`: page identity is not a host policy. Nor does it touch a trailing slash you write yourself (`{{absUrl '/courses/'}}` is still `/courses/`) or a file extension.

One consequence worth knowing: on Firebase with `cleanUrls` + `trailingSlash: false`, `about.html` and `about/index.html` are both served at `/about`, so `extensionLess` stops being a URL decision there and becomes purely an output-path one. On Netlify the two shapes stay distinct.

**The redirect encoding** (`redirects.format`, default `'netlify'`). `_redirects` is read by Netlify and Cloudflare Pages. Firebase Hosting ignores it entirely — it reads a `redirects` array in `firebase.json` — and Vercel reads `vercel.json`, so on those hosts the default writes a file nothing serves while your old URLs keep 404ing. Set `format` to `'firebase'` or `'vercel'` for a fragment to merge, `'none'` to opt out, or a writer function for anything else; `<build>/redirects.json` and `report().redirects.rules` carry the same rules as data whatever you choose. See `## Checking a build`.

## Helpers

Registered on `kiss.handlebars` for every instance; register your own on the same object.

**Layouts come first, and they are not kiss's.** Every multi-page site is structured by three block
helpers that `handlebars-layouts` registers on the same environment — they are not in the list below
because kiss does not define them, which is exactly why they were previously impossible to find here.
A layout in `config.folders.layouts` declares the slots:

```hbs
<!doctype html><html><head><title>{{title}}</title>{{#block "head"}}{{/block}}</head>
<body>{{#block "body"}}<p>fallback shown when a page fills nothing</p>{{/block}}</body></html>
```

and a page view fills them:

```hbs
{{#extend "layout"}}
  {{#content "body"}}<h1>{{title}}</h1>{{/content}}
  {{#content "head" mode="append"}}<link rel="stylesheet" href="/{{asset "css/site.css"}}">{{/content}}
{{/extend}}
```

`{{#block}}` defines a named slot and renders its own body when no page fills it; `{{#extend}}` names
the layout (the registered partial name, so `layouts/main.hbs` is `"main"`); `{{#content}}` fills one
slot. `mode` is `"replace"` (the default), `"append"` or `"prepend"` — append is how a page adds its
own stylesheet or JSON-LD to a shared `head` without discarding the layout's. Layouts and partials
share one namespace and are registered together (see `## Pages`), so a layout can `{{> "partial"}}`
like anything else, and editing one re-renders the pages that rendered it.

- `markdown` — block (`{{#markdown}}...{{/markdown}}`) or string/model value (`{{markdown model.body}}`); rendered through `kiss.remarkable`, returned as safe HTML. `undefined` logs a warning and renders nothing; a `null`, plain object or array also renders nothing (with a warning), rather than throwing.
- `sass` — file path string (`{{{sass "src/assets/main.scss"}}}`) and/or an inline block (`{{#sass}}$c: red; body { color: $c; }{{/sass}}`); both may be combined. A relative file path resolves against **`process.cwd()`**, not `config.folders.assets` or the view's own location; an absolute path is used as given. `style` is `'expanded'` in `dev: true`, `'compressed'` otherwise; `loadPaths` comes from `config.sass.includePaths`.
- `offset(index)` — returns `index + 1`, for 1-based numbering: `{{offset @index}}` inside a `{{#each}}`.
- `stringify(obj)` — `JSON.stringify(obj, null, 3)`; `{{{stringify this}}}` to inspect what's in scope (triple braces — it's JSON, not HTML to escape).
- `lookup` — Handlebars' built-in `lookup`, plus a warning when the key is undefined: `lookup: 'moodleAccess' is undefined in handbooks/uob.hbs` (the view is named when the page context carries one, once per page per key). Return value and prototype-access safety are the built-in's, unchanged — a dynamic partial `{{> (lookup . 'key')}}` with a missing key still fails the build with `The partial undefined could not be found`; you now also get the key's name.
- `isActive` — block helper for nav active-state: `{{#isActive page href="/about"}}class="active"{{/isActive}}`. **`page` there is not a keyword — it is the page context, passed positionally**, and that matters the moment the nav is data-driven: inside an `{{#each}}` the surrounding context is one level up, so it is `{{#each nav}}{{#isActive ../page href=href}}{{label}}{{/isActive}}{{/each}}`. Omitting it is not an error (Handlebars passes its own options object and the helper finds the block by shape), which is why the mistake is quiet. Hash keys: `href` (the link's path; an omitted or absent key is treated as `''`, not thrown on), `active` (default `'active'`, the string rendered as `{{active}}` inside the block when matched), `folderMatch` (default `false`). Both `href` and the page's own URL are reduced to the same key first — no leading/trailing slash, no file extension, no trailing `index` segment — so `href="/about"` matches the page whether it built to `about.html` or (`extensionLess: true`) `about/index.html`, and `/about`/`/about/` are always the same href. Exact key match by default; `folderMatch=true` also matches any page below `href` (`/blog` then matches `/blog/post-1`), and an empty `href` under `folderMatch` matches the home page only. A non-block usage, or a page context with no `pageURL`, logs a warning and renders the block as not-active rather than throwing.
- `canonical` — the current page's absolute URL: `{{canonical}}` → `https://example.com/about` for the page that built to `about.html`, `https://example.com/courses/` for the one that built to `courses/index.html`, and `https://example.com/` for the home page. **A directory index keeps a trailing slash by default** — that is the URL Netlify serves, and it answers the bare `/courses` with a 301, so the slashed form is the one that returns 200 there. **This is host policy, not a universal**: set `links: { trailingSlash: false }` for a host that serves the bare form (see `## Host URL policy`), and every URL kiss emits for that page loses the slash together. Under `extensionLess: true` every page but the home page builds to `<path>/<slug>/index.html` and so is a directory index too: its canonical is `https://example.com/about/`, again the URL the host serves without a redirect. Built from `config.siteUrl` and the page's own URL by the same code that writes `sitemap.xml`, so `<link rel="canonical" href="{{canonical}}">` and that page's `<loc>` are always the same string: extension dropped, a trailing `index` segment becoming the trailing slash, no double slash whether or not `siteUrl` ends in one. A page that overrides `siteUrl` for itself (`.page({ config: { siteUrl } })`) gets a canonical URL on that domain. It takes no arguments; `{{canonical this}}`, the shape a hand-rolled v1 helper usually had, works too. With no `siteUrl` it renders nothing and logs one warning per page; so does a render with no page context.
- `absUrl` — `config.siteUrl` joined to any site-relative path: `{{absUrl "/img/card.png"}}` → `https://example.com/img/card.png` (for `og:image`, an RSS link, a feed). `/about` and `about` are both `https://example.com/about`; a trailing slash is preserved, not trimmed (`about/` → `https://example.com/about/`), and a trailing `index` segment becomes one (`/courses/index.html` → `https://example.com/courses/`); a file extension is kept (`css/site.css` stays `css/site.css`, unlike `canonical`'s page URL); a path that already has a scheme (`https://cdn.example/x.png`) is returned untouched, `siteUrl` or not; `{{absUrl}}` with no path is `{{canonical}}`. A non-string path logs a warning and renders nothing.
- `asset` — the path of a file `.copyAssets()` put in the build, under whatever cache-busting policy `config.assets` sets: `{{asset "css/site.css"}}` renders `css/site.css` with no policy, `css/site.a1b2c3d4.css` under `assets: { hash: true }`, and `css/site.css?v=1.4.5` under `assets: { version: '1.4.5' }`. The template says which file it wants; the config says how it is cached, so changing the policy never touches a template. Ask for the path the file has when nothing is renaming it — a `.scss` source by its compiled `.css` name (`css/site.css`, not `css/site.scss`) — with or without a leading slash. It renders **no leading slash**, so the template picks the base: `href="/{{asset "css/site.css"}}"` for a root-relative link, `href="{{root}}{{asset "css/site.css"}}"` for one that also works opened off the file system, and `{{absUrl (asset "css/site.css")}}` for an absolute URL (the query string and the hashed extension both survive). A URL that already has a scheme is passed through untouched. A space in a filename is fine end to end — manifest, helper and the broken-link scan all handle it — so an asset named `hand-in-hand-for syria.png` needs no rename. A path that is not in the build renders as you wrote it and logs one warning per page naming it, rather than failing the page; a non-string path logs a warning and renders nothing.
- `link` — the URL of a page **by its identity**, so a template never guesses one: `<a href="{{link "about"}}">` renders `/about.html`, or `/about/` on an `extensionLess` site, and `{{link "blog/post" slug=post.slug}}` renders that post's path. Every page has an `id` — by default its view's route without the extension (`blog/listing.hbs` → `blog/listing`), and for a `.pages()` item the registration's route (or its `id`) plus the item's slug (`blog/post/the-cascara-experiment`) — and `id:` on the page options (or on a fan-out **record**) sets it yourself. What it renders is the path the host actually serves: `/`, `/about.html`, `/courses/`, `/blog/the-cascara-experiment/`, `/data/index.json`. It is **root-relative**: for a site served from a path prefix, or a link that has to be absolute (an `og:url`, a feed), use `{{link "about" absolute=true}}` → `https://example.com/about.html`; for the pretty form the sitemap and `{{canonical}}` emit, `{{link "about" canonical=true}}` → `/about` (or `absolute=true` alongside it for `https://example.com/about`). A site whose host serves the pretty form on every page sets `links: { canonical: true }` once instead of writing `canonical=true` at every call site; the per-call hash still wins either way, `canonical=false` included, and `canonical` and `absolute` compose — with both, the link is the absolute URL of the pretty path. **It is the one helper that fails the build**: an id no page claims, an id two pages' *defaults* both arrived at (neither keeps it — a `notice` names the views and asks you to set one), or a page with `generate: false` (which claims no id) fails the page that linked it, naming the id and the view that asked — a link is a promise, and unlike a hand-written path it is checkable at render. Under `dev: true` it warns and renders `#` instead, so the live preview shows you both the page and the mistake. Two pages claiming the same **explicit** id fail the build outright, like two pages claiming one output path.
- `env` — block helper gated on `config.dev`: `{{#env is="dev"}}dev-only{{else}}prod-only{{/env}}`. Hash key: `is` (required string, case-insensitive substring match — `"dev"`/`"prod"`). A missing or non-string `is` logs an error and renders neither branch.

## Writing llms.txt

`llms.txt` is the curated, AI-facing index of a site — what an answer engine reads before it crawls. `.llms()` builds one from the pages already registered, so it cannot list a URL the site does not serve or a title the page does not carry. End to end:

```js
kiss
  .page({ view: 'index.hbs', title: 'A1K9 Training', description: 'Dog training and behaviour work in South Wales' })
  .pages({ view: 'courses/course.hbs', model: 'courses', path: 'courses' })
  .page({ view: 'rota.hbs', ignoreLlms: true }) // in the sitemap, out of the index
  .generate()
  .sitemap()
  .llms({
    title: 'A1K9 Training',
    // Inline text, or a path to a file: `summary: 'src/content/summary.md'`
    summary: 'Dog behaviour and obedience training in South Wales, run by Gaynor Probert.',
    sections: { root: 'Pages', courses: 'Courses' },
    notes: 'src/content/llms-notes.md',
  })
```

writes:

```markdown
# A1K9 Training

> Dog behaviour and obedience training in South Wales, run by Gaynor Probert.

## Pages

- [A1K9 Training](https://a1k9training.co.uk/): Dog training and behaviour work in South Wales

## Courses

- [Bronze obedience](https://a1k9training.co.uk/courses/bronze-obedience): Six weeks, group class
```

## Checking a build

`npx kiss-ssg check <script> [args…]` runs a site's own build script as a dry run: the build is staged and then discarded, so the build folder is neither emptied nor written, and what you get back is the verdict instead of the output. (`npx kiss-ssg aikb <script>` is the same run with one thing added — see **Recording the knowledge base** below. Both take `--summary`, `--against <file>` and `--help`.) Arguments after the script are passed through to it, so a site that takes a season or a cohort is checked the way it is run. It prints a JSON array with one report per `Kiss` instance the script created — a script that builds several outputs gets several reports:

```json
[
  {
    "ok": false,
    "mode": "check",
    "buildDir": "./public",
    "duration": 160,
    "pages": [
      {
        "view": "index.hbs",
        "buildTo": "./public/index.html",
        "ok": true,
        "hash": "9c1185a5c5e9fc54612808977ee8f548b2258d31"
      }
    ],
    "failures": [
      {
        "view": "stockists/stockist.hbs [item 3: harbour-market-stall]",
        "buildTo": null,
        "message": "Incomplete stockist record — missing address"
      }
    ],
    "assets": [{ "source": "css/site.css", "target": "css/site.605b52d7.css" }],
    "sitemap": "./public/sitemap.xml",
    "pipeline": [{ "name": "tailwind", "ok": true, "duration": 420 }],
    "llms": "./public/llms.txt",
    "aikb": {
      "folder": "AIKB",
      "written": false,
      "notes": {
        "missing": ["AIKB/notes/controllers/stockist.md"],
        "dead": ["AIKB/notes/pipeline/postcss.md"],
        "stale": ["AIKB/notes/pipeline/tailwind.md"],
        "dangling": ["AIKB/notes/pipeline/tailwind.md: src/assets/old.css"]
      },
      "subjects": [
        {
          "kind": "controllers",
          "id": "stockist.js",
          "note": "notes/controllers/stockist.md",
          "hash": "9f2a1c4e8b70d3a6c5e1f08b2d47a93c6e5b1d20"
        },
        {
          "kind": "pipeline",
          "id": "tailwind",
          "note": "notes/pipeline/tailwind.md",
          "hash": "3c81be07f4a2d95e6b0c7f13a8d24e59b6710fc8"
        }
      ]
    },
    "links": {
      "checked": 24,
      "broken": [{ "page": "./public/about.html", "href": "/news/gone" }]
    },
    "redirects": {
      "file": "./public/_redirects",
      "aliases": 2,
      "removed": ["/news/autumn-2025.html"],
      "collisions": [],
      "moved": [
        { "id": "blog/post", "from": "/blog/old-slug/", "to": "/blog/new-slug/" }
      ]
    },
    "feed": "./public/feed.xml"
  }
]
```

**Exit code 1** if any report is `ok: false`, if the script itself exited non-zero, or if no report was written at all — a script that never awaits `complete()` reports nothing, which is itself the finding. Exit 0 with `ok: true` on every report is the only passing result. The site's own build log goes to stderr, so stdout is nothing but the JSON. `--summary` prints one line per site instead (`ok ./public (check) — 6 pages, 0 failed, 2 assets, 153ms`, plus a line per failure, then — for a site with a knowledge base — the four note findings, one line each: `  note missing: <path>` per subject nobody has explained, `  note dead: <path>` per note whose subject is gone, `  note stale: <path>` per note whose stamp is no longer its subject's hash, and `  note dangling: <path>: <token>` per file reference in a note that resolves to nothing — and then `  broken link: <page> -> <href>` per internal reference that resolves to nothing, `  removed without redirect: <path>` per page the last record wrote that this build does not and no alias covers, `  moved without redirect: <from> -> <to> (<id>)` per page the record and this build share an `id` with whose path changed and whose old path no alias covers, and `  alias collides with a page: <path>` per alias a live page already answers — the two rename findings name **served URLs** (`/courses/`, `/about.html`, `/`), the addresses a reader's links carry, never the `index.html` files behind them; none of them changes the exit code); it is read wherever you write it, and a site that needs the word `--summary` itself takes it after a bare `--`. `--against <file>` (before the script, and it takes the next word as its file) names the baseline for the diff described below; a site that has recorded a knowledge base is diffed against it **without** the flag.

**`check` diffs this build against an earlier one.** With no flag, the baseline is the site's own `<config.folders.aikb>/last-build.json` when that file exists — the state of the site when its knowledge base was last recorded, so the answer is "what has changed since that piece of work closed" rather than "since somebody last ran a build". `--against <file>` names a different baseline and always wins. The file is a report somebody kept: a `KISS_REPORT` JSON Lines file, the JSON array `check` itself prints, or a single report object — all three are read, so you do not have to say which you have. Reports are paired by `buildDir` (a script that builds several sites gets several diffs), pages are matched by output path and compared by `hash`, so the answer is about the bytes a browser would receive rather than about which files were touched. A page whose `hash` is `null` on either side counts as changed, never as unchanged. Under `--summary` the diff prints under that site's line:

```
ok ./public (check) — 6 pages, 0 failed, 2 assets, 153ms
  ~ asset css/site.css -> css/site.136acc63.css (was css/site.e7abc083.css)
  + ./public/news/spring-2026.html
  - ./public/news/autumn-2025.html
  ~ ./public/news/index.html
  = 3 unchanged
```

Without `--summary` stdout becomes `{ "reports": [...], "diff": [...] }` instead of the bare array whenever there is a diff to print — under `--against`, or under `check` with a recorded baseline — and `diff` is in the same order as `reports`, one entry each: `{ buildDir, added, removed, changed, unchanged, assets }`, the three page lists holding output paths, sorted. A missing or unreadable file is a usage error (exit 1, nothing built). The diff never changes the exit code: it describes the build, it does not judge it.

**Assets that moved are named under the pages.** Whenever a diff has pages in it, `formatDiff` **opens** with one `  ~ asset <source> -> <target> (was <target>)` row per emitted asset whose filename changed — above the page rows, capped at ten with `  … and N more assets changed` — and `diff[].assets` carries the same rows as `{ source, from, to }`. This exists because of `assets.hash`: a hashed stylesheet's filename **is** its content hash, so one changed asset rewrites the `<link href>` of every page that references it and the diff reads `~ <every page>, = 0 unchanged` with nothing in any page source to explain it. The row names the cause, and it goes first because that is where the reader already is: after a two-hundred-page list it would be a footnote reached by scrolling past everything it explains. Only assets both builds emitted are rows — one the baseline never saw has no previous name to have moved from — and nothing is printed when no page moved, since the rows are there to explain a diff rather than to be one.

**Driving it without the bin** (a CI step, a harness of your own): `KISS_CHECK=1` turns any build into a check — `cleanBuild` becomes `'atomic'`, `dev` becomes `false`, and the staging folder is discarded when `complete()` settles whether the build passed or failed, so nothing published is touched. Any value counts as set except `0`, `false` and the empty string. `KISS_REPORT=<file>` appends each settled build's report to `<file>` as JSON Lines, one line per `Kiss` instance. `KISS_AIKB=1` (same rule again) is what `kiss-ssg aikb` adds on top of those two. None of the three changes the script's own exit code — that is the caller's decision, and the bin's.

One thing a check deliberately does do: it runs `config.assets.pipeline` exactly as a build does, so it is not read-only over your working tree — the steps regenerate whatever they generate, into your source, which is why there is nothing extra for the check to discard.

**Broken internal links.** Every settled non-dev build scans its own output and reports what it found as `report().links` — `{ checked, broken: [{ page, href }] }`, and one `  broken link: <page> -> <href>` line per finding under `--summary`. **Checked:** the `href`, `src`, each `srcset` candidate and `action` of every `a`, `link`, `script`, `img`, `source`, `video`, `audio`, `iframe` and `form` the page wrote — resolved root-relative against the build folder and relative against the page's own directory, accepting a file that is there, a page this build wrote, `<path>/` → `<path>/index.html`, an extension-less `<path>` → `<path>.html` or `<path>/index.html`, and an asset under the name `{{asset}}` actually emitted.
