An absolute URL on your own `siteUrl` is **internal** — that is what catches a renamed slug still linked from a nav or a `{{canonical}}`. **Ignored:** another origin, a protocol-relative `//host/x`, `mailto:`, `tel:`, `data:`, `javascript:`, a bare `#fragment` and an empty value; a query string and a fragment are stripped before resolving. **`{{link}}` and the checker are two halves of one thing:** the helper renders a path the resolver accepts by construction — a file, a `<path>/` directory index, or `/` — so a site whose internal hrefs are all `{{link}}` reports `broken: []`, and the scan stays the net for the hand-written references beside them. One qualifier: the pages the scan knows about are the ones that **wrote bytes**, so a `{{link}}` to a page that failed to render *is* reported broken on every page that linked it — which is the honest answer, since no such file was published. Under `assets.hash` a hardcoded `/css/site.css` **is** a finding: the file on disk is `css/site.<hash>.css`, so use `{{asset}}`. The finding is advisory — it never changes `ok` and never changes the exit code. `links: { check: false }` turns the scan off, and a **dev build or a watch rebuild always reports `links: null`**: a scoped re-render has not rewritten every page, so there is nothing honest to scan.

**Redirects, and what a rename left behind.** A page's `aliases` are the old URL paths it now answers. An alias is a fact about the site and is portable; the file it is written into is one vendor's encoding of that fact, so every settled build with an alias writes `<build>/redirects.json` — `{ version, rules: [{ from, to, status }] }`, the host-neutral list, **always**, where `status` is **always `301`** (it is in the data so a consumer need not hardcode it; there is no way to ask for a `302`, `308` or `410`, and no forced/wildcard rules) — and then whatever host encodings `config.redirects.format` names beside it.

**`format` is unset by default and takes a list.** Unset (`null`) writes the IR and no host file: kiss does not guess where you deploy. Because v2.3 always wrote `_redirects`, a build that has aliases and has not set `format` logs one `notice` naming the fix — an explicit `'none'` or `[]` is a decision and is silent. A bare string or function is a list of one, and `['netlify', 'firebase']` emits **both** host files from the one build, which is what a site with Netlify previews and Firebase production needs. Duplicates collapse; order is kept. `'netlify'` is `<build>/_redirects`, one `/<old> <new> 301` per line, sorted and byte-stable. `'firebase'`, `'vercel'` and `'htaccess'` write a **fragment to merge** (`redirects.firebase.json`, `redirects.vercel.json`, `redirects.htaccess` — the last using mod_alias `Redirect`, not `RewriteRule`, so a `.` in an alias stays literal) — the `redirects` array alone, because your `firebase.json` holds hosting targets, headers and rewrites that are yours, and kiss will not rewrite it. `'none'` is a readable spelling of the empty list. A function is a custom writer: `(rules, { buildDir, config }) => [{ file, contents }]`, paths relative to the build folder, and one that throws fails the build rather than silently writing nothing. An unknown format name throws at `new Kiss()` — every entry of a list is checked, so one typo in an array of four is named rather than quietly dropped. In every case `<new>` is the page's canonical path (`/`, `/courses/`, `/about`), the same string its `{{canonical}}` and its `<loc>` carry. No meta-refresh. A site with no aliases writes **no file at all**, so a hand-written `_redirects` you keep in `src/assets/` is copied into the build and left alone. An alias is one path: one with a space or a line break inside it is dropped, because the file is space-separated columns and one rule per line. If the file cannot be written the build fails, as a page that cannot be written fails it. `report().redirects` is `{ file, aliases, removed, collisions, moved, rules, json, formats, files }` (`formats` is the list that ran, `[]` for IR-only, `'custom'` per writer function; `file` is the **first** host file and `files` is the complete, authoritative list), or `null` when there is nothing to say — no alias anywhere in the site, no removal and no move, which is the ordinary answer for a site that uses neither feature and for a recorded site nothing has happened to. Three advisory findings ride with it. `removed` names the pages the **last record** (`<config.folders.aikb>/last-build.json`, written by `npx kiss-ssg aikb`) wrote that this build does not, minus any an alias now covers — a page that vanished with no redirect. Both rename findings name the page's **served URL** — `/courses/` for a directory index, `/about.html` for a file page, `/` for the home page — because that is what a reader's link says and what an `aliases` entry has to match; the comparison behind them is made on the output files. It is the one finding that needs a record: without one it is empty, and an unreadable one is treated the same way. Paths on both sides are compared build-relative, so a record made from one working directory and a check run from another still agree. `moved` names the pages the last record and this build both have — paired by the page's `id`, not by its path — whose output path changed and whose old path no alias covers: `{ id, from, to }` per page as served URLs, sorted by `from`, and one `notice` each carrying the fix (`add "<from>" to that page's aliases`). It needs a record too, and it needs an id on **both** sides: a page whose identity is stable is one this finding can follow across a rename, and a page whose identity changed with it is not. That is a real limit — a `.pages()` item's default id embeds its slug (`blog/post/<slug>`), so renaming a post's slug changes its id as well as its path and the event is reported as a `removed` instead. `moved` is for pages with a stable id: a `.page()` page whose `path`, `slug` or `ext` moved, and any page (a fan-out record included) that carries an explicit `id`. A move suppresses the matching `removed`, so one rename is one finding. `collisions` names the aliases a live page already answers — its canonical path (`/about`) or the file itself (`/about.html`) — because on both hosts a non-forced rule at a source a real file occupies is **silently ignored**, doing nothing at all; an alias two pages both claim is listed for the same reason. Neither moves `ok` or the exit code.

Two things a check cannot make true. A site that **reads its own build folder back** after `complete()` (an index that lists the version folders on disk) sees a folder nothing was published into, so it reports fewer of them than a real build would. And a site with `cleanBuild: false` that relies on files an **earlier** build left behind starts from an empty staging folder, since check mode stages everything.

### Recording the knowledge base

`npx kiss-ssg aikb <script> [args…]` writes the site's own knowledge base into `config.folders.aikb` (default `./AIKB`): a map of the site as the build saw it, for the developer who comes back to it in two years. It runs exactly the build `check` runs — staged and discarded, publishing nothing — and the folder is the only thing it leaves behind. Nothing else writes it: there is no API call, and an ordinary build, a `check`, a dev build and a watch rebuild all write none of it. Recording is a **ceremony**: run it when a piece of work is finished, and commit the folder. That is what makes the diff above mean "since this work opened" instead of "since the last time anybody built".

**It refuses to record a build that did not work.** A failed build writes nothing and the summary says `  not recorded — build failed`; the exit code is `check`'s. A dev build (`dev: true`) writes nothing either. The previous record stays exactly as it was — a knowledge base that describes a broken build is worse than a slightly old one.

**Four files, all byte-stable across two identical records** — nothing is timestamped and every list is sorted, so recording an unchanged site twice leaves `git status` clean and any diff in the folder is a real change to the shape of the site:

| File              | Written                      | What it holds                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `README.md`       | once, if absent; never again | what the folder is, which files are generated, how to write and stamp a note, what the four findings mean, and what `site.md` is for                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| `site-map.md`     | every record                 | the map as markdown: the site's URL, build folder and source folders; a row per page (output path, the page's `id`, view, model source, controller source, the partials and layouts it actually rendered); the partial → pages index; models and controllers with the pages that used them; the asset pipeline's steps; and a `## Subjects` table (kind, subject, its note, the first 12 characters of its hash). The Pages table's `Id` column is the list of ids `{{link}}` answers to on this site — the autocomplete for an agent adding a page or linking to one |
| `site-map.json`   | every record                 | the same map as data, including `subjects` with each subject's whole hash — what a note's `subject-hash` stamp is copied from                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| `last-build.json` | every record                 | that build's report with every timing dropped — the baseline `check` diffs against                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

The folder is **source, meant to be committed**: it sits outside `config.folders.build`, survives `cleanBuild`, and is not created at all until you record one. Setting `folders.aikb: null` switches it off entirely.

**Having the folder is not the same as opting in.** A build reports `report().aikb` when `folders.aikb` is set *and* `<folder>/site-map.json` is there — the one file only a record writes. Until then `aikb` is `null` and nothing is built: the default `./AIKB` is harmless in a repository whose `AIKB/` is something else (hand-written module notes, say). Once a site has recorded, every build — including a `check` — reports the folder and the note findings, with `written: false`.

**Notes are yours; the engine never writes one.** A map says what the site is; a note says why, which no build can work out. Three kinds of subject carry judgement and each wants a note under `AIKB/notes/`, at a path derived mechanically from its id: a controller **file** (`stockist.js` → `notes/controllers/stockist.md`), a model fetched by **URL** (`https://api.example.com/v2/events?x=1` → `notes/models/api.example.com-v2-events.md`, host and path, query dropped) and an **asset pipeline step** (`tailwind` → `notes/pipeline/tailwind.md`). Plain pages, partials and `.json` models are deliberately not subjects — a note saying "renders the about page" is noise. An inline controller or an object model has no file to attach a note to and is not a subject either.

**Every subject carries a hash, and a note may be stamped with it.** `site-map.json`'s `subjects` is `{ kind, id, note, hash }` per subject, sorted, and `site-map.md` has the same as a `## Subjects` table (the hash shortened to 12 characters): sha1 of the controller file's bytes, or of the pipeline step's `run` string, and `null` for a URL model — whose id *is* the subject, so there is nothing for a hash to add. Copy that hash into the note's frontmatter as `subject-hash: <sha1>` when you write or review the note:

```markdown
---
subject-hash: 9f2a1c4e8b70d3a6c5e1f08b2d47a93c6e5b1d20
---

## What it does
```

The engine never writes a stamp, and an unstamped note is never reported stale — stamping is opt-in, per note. The hash to stamp with is on **every** build's report as `report().aikb.subjects`, not only on a record's: at the moment a stale note is found, `site-map.json` on disk still describes the previous record, so the report is the only place the current hash exists.

**Four findings, on `report().aikb.notes`, every build.** **missing** — a subject with no note. **dead** — a note under `notes/` whose subject is not in the map. **stale** — a note whose `subject-hash` stamp is not its subject's current hash (a URL model can never be stale). **dangling** — `"<note path>: <token>"` for a backticked token in a note that looks like a file reference and resolves to nothing: not a file on disk, not a page view or output path, not a partial name, a model or controller name, a folder in the map, or a path under the AIKB folder. The dangling filter is deliberately narrow — a token needs a `/` or a known extension, and must hold no spaces, `<`, `>`, `*`, `{`, `}` or `$`; fenced code blocks, trailing-slash folders and anything with a URI scheme are skipped — because a lint that fires on every note is one people learn to ignore. None of the four is a build failure and none changes an exit code.

**`AIKB/site.md` is the page about the whole site**, rather than about any one subject: authored, evergreen, and never written by the engine. It is scanned for `dangling` references when it is there, and checked for nothing else. The generated `AIKB/README.md` names its five sections — What this site is and who for · How it is deployed · Conventions · Standing gotchas · Retired feedback — and the `kiss-memory-consolidate` skill is what maintains it.

A recorded folder to read: [examples/9-migrated-from-v1/AIKB/](examples/9-migrated-from-v1/AIKB/) — recorded with `cd examples && npx kiss-ssg aikb 9-migrated-from-v1.js`, with one authored note beside the map.

## Docs

- [README.md](README.md): full usage docs, worked examples for `.page()`/`.pages()`/`.sitemap()`, the helpers list.
- [examples/](examples/): ships in the package, so an agent working in a consuming project can read `node_modules/kiss-ssg/examples/README.md` and run a copy from there. Two tiers. Examples 1–6 and 10 are the feature reference, one idea each — scan, page/model/controller, `.pages()` fan-out, layouts and partials, helpers, the three site-level files (`sitemap.xml`, `llms.txt` and a generated `robots.txt` whose `Sitemap:` line comes from the same registry), and an external tool in `config.assets.pipeline`. Examples 7–9 and 11 are exemplars, whole sites to copy by shape rather than a single feature: 7 is versioned outputs, one build per season; 8 is a site built from a folder of records with one broken one, fed and validated in the controller; 9 is every v1 → v2 migration recipe as running code, in a site that builds clean, and it ships the recorded `AIKB/` folder (see **Recording the knowledge base**); 11 is a blog — posts as a folder fan-out with a controller file, a paginated listing at `/blog/` and `/blog/page/2/`, tag pages as a second fan-out over a computed array, `.feed({ section: 'blog' })`, `.robots()`, one renamed post whose record carries `aliases` so `redirects.json` and `_redirects` are both written (`redirects: { format: 'netlify' }` names the host), and a recorded `AIKB/` with two authored notes. Every example builds and exits by default (`node examples/<N>-name.js`, or `npm run eg<N>`); pass `--dev` to run examples 1–6, 8, 9, 10 and 11 as a live dev server instead (7 takes a season slug in place of `--dev`). Example 8 is the only one that exits non-zero, and it does so on purpose; example 11 takes `--broken`, which adds one bad link so a `check` reports exactly one `broken link:` finding.
- [types/](types/): TypeScript declarations, generated from the JSDoc in `lib/` and shipped in the package (`package.json`'s `types`, and an `exports` map whose `.` entry resolves `types` → `./types/kiss.d.ts` and both `import` and `require` → `./lib/kiss.js`). A plain-JavaScript site gets full completion and checking by putting `// @ts-check` at the top of its build script — no TypeScript, no `@types/` package. Every option type is reachable from the one entry: `/** @type {import('kiss-ssg').KissConfigInput} */` on the config object, `import('kiss-ssg').PageOptions` / `PagesOptions` on page options, `import('kiss-ssg').KissController` on a controller, and `import('kiss-ssg').BuildError` to cast the error `complete()` rejects with before reading `err.failures`. Also exported: `KissConfig` (the resolved config a view sees), `KissFolders`, `PageOptionsPatch` (what a controller returns), `BuildData`, `BuildFailure`, `BuildReport` (what `report()` returns) with `BuildPage`, `BuildAsset` and `BuildReportFailure`, `SitemapOptions`, `SitemapUrl`, `LlmsOptions`, `WatchOptions`. Arbitrary keys are allowed on the config and on page options — they reach the template — so only the documented keys are checked; `folders` is closed, so a misspelled folder name is an error.
- **The two plugins below are NOT in this npm package.** `package.json`'s `files` whitelist ships `bin/`, `lib/`, `types/`, `llms.txt`, `AIKB/` and `examples/` — so if you are reading this from `node_modules/kiss-ssg/`, the `plugins/` links that follow do not resolve on your disk and nothing in the installed package will tell you the skills exist. They are installed from the marketplace, not from the tarball: `/plugin marketplace add cprobert/kiss-ssg`, then the `/plugin install` line on each bullet. Worth doing before a migration — a real conversion was completed without them purely because an agent inside a consuming project had no way to learn they were there.
- [plugins/kiss-ssg/](plugins/kiss-ssg/) (marketplace only, see above): a Claude Code plugin, installed with `/plugin marketplace add cprobert/kiss-ssg` then `/plugin install kiss-ssg@kiss-ssg`. Four skills, each named `kiss-<something>` for easy discovery — `kiss-site-new`, `kiss-page-add`, `kiss-site-migrate`, `kiss-build-check` — which sequence this file and the examples rather than restating them, and whose descriptions are written so Claude reaches for them on its own without being invoked by name. The plugin does not ship in the npm tarball, only in the repository; a project's CLAUDE.md can import this file directly with `@node_modules/kiss-ssg/llms.txt`.
- [plugins/kiss-memory/](plugins/kiss-memory/) (marketplace only, see above): the sibling plugin from the same marketplace (`/plugin install kiss-memory@kiss-ssg`). Five skills: `kiss-site-brief` (the returning-developer briefing over the recorded `AIKB/`, every statement labelled generated or recollection), `kiss-branch-open`, `kiss-branch-pulse` and `kiss-branch-close` (a piece of work on a site, verified against the `check` diff, with the close the only moment `kiss-ssg aikb` records), and `kiss-memory-consolidate` (folds session logs into `AIKB/site.md` and repairs the notes `check` reports as stale, dangling or dead).
- [lib/](lib/): the engine — `kiss.js` (orchestrator, public API), `kiss-page.js` (one page's render), and one module per concern (`config`, `logger`, `handlebars-helpers`, `partials`, `dependency-graph`, `assets`, `asset-manifest`, `sass`, `model-resolver`, `fetch-policy`, `controller-resolver`, `sitemap`, `dev-server`, `watcher`, `utils`, `build-report`, `check`, `pipeline`, `llms`, `aikb`). Per-module notes: [AIKB/](AIKB/).

## Migrating from v1

- **Node ≥22.12.0 first** (`package.json` `engines.node`) — check this before anything else: v2 will not install or run below it. If your project pins a dev Node version the way this repo's own `.nvmrc` does, bump yours before touching any code.
- ESM-only (`import Kiss from 'kiss-ssg'`); CJS `require()` still works on Node ≥22.12.
- `folders.root` and `folders.static` are gone — no module ever read them, so a config passing them gets nothing rather than a quiet no-op; delete the keys. The six keys v2 derives from `folders.src`/`folders.build` unless overridden (`pages`, `assets`, `layouts`, `partials`, `models`, `controllers`) are documented in `## Config` above.
- The `generate` callback now fires after files are written, not before.
- v1 logged a page's render/write failure and resolved anyway; v2's `complete()` rejects with an `AggregateError` listing the failed views (`err.failures` = `[{ view, buildTo, error }]`). The v1 callback-style idiom — `kiss.generate(function () { this.complete(function () { ... }) })` — now leaves that rejection unhandled the first time a page fails, so give `complete()` a `.catch`:
  ```js
  kiss
    .scan()
    .generate()
    .complete()
    .catch((err) => {
      for (const f of err.failures) {
        console.error(`${f.view} | ${f.buildTo} | ${f.error.message}`)
      }
      process.exitCode = 1
    })
  ```
  A failed build never runs `complete()`'s own callback, so anything you did there — writing a sitemap, generating an index, kicking off a deploy — has to run again in the `catch`. And a chain that ends at `.generate()` with no `.complete()` never sees any of this: it keeps exiting 0 on a broken build, so every deploy script must `await complete()` (or otherwise attach a rejection handler to it) to catch a failure.
- Handlebars is per-instance — register helpers on `kiss.handlebars`, not the global `handlebars` module. Partials are registered there too, so a helper reading the global `handlebars.partials` renders nothing; use `kiss.handlebars.partials` or the native dynamic partial `{{> (lookup this "name")}}`. Every entry of `kiss.handlebars.partials` is a function — a compiled template that also records which page invoked it — so a helper that renders an entry by name must accept a function; the one-line form is under `.registerPartials()` above.
- `utils` and the redirect renderers are named exports (`import { utils, renderRedirects } from 'kiss-ssg'`), not `kiss-ssg/libs/utils.js` or `kiss-ssg/lib/redirects.js`. The `exports` map has one entry, so any deep path into the package (`kiss-ssg/lib/…`, `kiss-ssg/libs/…`) now fails with `ERR_PACKAGE_PATH_NOT_EXPORTED` instead of half-working — everything public is reachable from `'kiss-ssg'` itself.
- Controllers may `export default` instead of `module.exports =`.
- Duplicate output paths, including `.pages()` fan-out where a controller yields the same slug twice, are no longer written twice: the second page is not built and the collision is a build failure, so `complete()` rejects naming the path (`Page already processed: <path>`) — v1 wrote whichever page came last. If you relied on that v1 skip to give one source priority over another — a low-priority fan-out registered last, on the assumption the engine would silently drop whatever slug a higher-priority source had already claimed — dedupe the slugs yourself before registering instead:
  ```js
  const claimed = new Set(catalogItems.map((c) => c.slug))
  const rdItems = allRdItems.filter((r) => !claimed.has(r.slug))
  kiss.pages({ view: 'rd.hbs', model: rdItems /* ... */ })
  ```
- **Upgrading from a v2 _prerelease_ rather than v1: `markdown.breaks` flipped.** It was hard-coded `true` in `2.0.0-alpha.5` and has been `false` since `2.0.0-beta.1`, where the option set became the configurable `DEFAULT_MARKDOWN` block; `2.0.0`, `2.1.0` and `2.2.x` all match beta.1. A project pinned to an alpha may carry a workaround for the old default — `kiss.remarkable.set({ breaks: false })` followed by `kiss.registerPartials()`, often with a comment asserting that v2 defaults to `breaks: true`. That comment was correct when it was written and has been wrong since beta.1: delete both calls and set `markdown: { breaks: true }` in config if you actually want the old behaviour. The `registerPartials()` half is why the pair survives upgrades unnoticed — it does not look redundant, because `.md` partials are rendered to HTML at registration and a later mutation of `kiss.remarkable` really would need a re-register to reach them.
- **Unchanged in v2**, so there is nothing to migrate here even though it looks load-bearing: the per-page `generate: false` option (default `true`) still skips building one page; `callback.call(this, ...)` still binds the `Kiss` instance inside `generate`/`complete`/`sitemap` callbacks; the per-page `ext` option; `copyAssets(sourceDir, targetDir)` to a second directory; `viewStats()`/`getModelByID()`. `_stack` (and any other underscore-prefixed field) is internal and unversioned — code reading `_stack[].buildTo`/`_stack[].page.options` works today by accident; `.sitemap()` is the supported way to enumerate registered pages.
